newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh defense admits making up "confession".
newsitem.headline: McVeigh defense admits making up "confession".

text.p: The lawyer for accused Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh says the defence made up a confession and attributed it to his client as a ploy to flush out a witness suspected of being involved in the bombing.
The alleged "confession" was obtained by the Dallas Morning News and published initially over the Internet on Friday, creating a media storm with its purported quotes from McVeigh.

It quoted the Gulf War veteran, who has pleaded innocent to planting the bomb which killed 168 people, as saying he was indeed the bomber and that he blew up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in daytime because, "we needed a body count to make our point."
McVeigh's chief attorney, Stephen Jones, at a press conference Monday accused the paper of breaking into the defence's computer system and stealing that document along with thousands of others.
He also denied that the sensational statement was a confession or "a legitimate defence document."

Jones refused at the press conference to explain why the defence had such a document in its possession, but that explanation came hours later when his office issued a statement received by Reuters Tuesday.

In the statement, Jones said the defence wanted to speak to a person with a "history of incitement to violence and criminal activity, (who) was suspected by the defence of being involved in the conspiracy to bomb the Murrah building."
It added, "The defence believed that this person was willing to talk if the individual believed that he was not suspected by the defence of being a participant in the bombing."

"The effort to interview this individual by a defence investigator was aided by two other persons, one of whom is now deceased and the other is an individual who writes frequently about the Oklahoma City bombing case. We can provide no other information before trial."

McVeigh is scheduled to go on trial in Denver March 31 for the April 19, 1995 bombing of the federal building, in which 168 people were killed and 500 injured. Officials call the explosion the worst act of terorrism committed on U.S. soil.

Jones said that as a result of the Dallas Morning News story he was considering asking for a 90-day delay in the start of the trial or even having a judge hear the case without a jury. But he said it would be several days before he made a decision.

He also called for legal action to be taken against the paper for allegedly breaking into the defence's computer system. The paper denied having stolen any documents, saying it obtained them through routine news gathering techniques. It also said that it had turned over all its documents to its lawyers and would not be publishing any more excerpts.

J.D. Cash, a reporter with the McCurtain Daily Gazette in Idabel, Oklahoma, a paper which has broken several stories on the case, said he had been shown the "confession" document at least a year ago by one of the defence investigators.
However, he said he could tell by the way it was written that the information was not legitimate. "I was told it was an investigative tool," Cash said.
